extraction_text: King Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what his son Duryodhana said after being defeated and having his thigh broken.
Sanjaya describes Duryodhana's condition: lying on the ground with broken thigh, head being stepped on, covered in dust, with disheveled hair.
Duryodhana angrily blames Bhima for defeating him through unfair means and violating combat rules.
Duryodhana laments that despite having powerful protectors like Bhishma, Karna, Drona, Ashwatthama, Shalya, and others, he still faced defeat due to fate.
Duryodhana accuses the Pandavas of committing cruel acts against warriors like Bhurishrava, Karna, Bhishma, and Drona.
Duryodhana questions whether victory obtained through deceit can bring true happiness to righteous people.
Duryodhana expresses humiliation at having his head stepped on by Bhima despite being a king who enjoyed prosperity among his people.
Duryodhana asks Sanjaya to convey his words to his parents (Dhritarashtra and Gandhari) who understand Kshatriya dharma.

Duryodhana recounts his achievements: performing sacrifices, ruling lands and oceans, standing over enemies, generosity to friends, conquering enemy territories, respecting relatives, and fulfilling life's duties.
Duryodhana questions whether anyone could be more fortunate than him despite his current defeat.
Duryodhana, mortally wounded, reflects on his life and achievements, declaring himself fortunate for his unvanquished status in battle, adherence to his dharma, and the honorable death he sought.
Duryodhana accuses Bhima of defeating him using unlawful means (adharma) in their mace duel.

Duryodhana instructs the messengers to deliver a final message to Ashvatthaman, Kritavarman, and Kripa, warning them not to trust the Pandavas, whom he calls destroyers of rules who have committed many evil deeds.

attributes.relationship: Duryodhana (Kaurava leader) to his remaining generals; Accusation against the Pandavas

extraction_text: Duryodhana states he will follow the departed souls of his allies (including Drona, Shalya, Karna, Bhurishrava, Shalya, Shalya, Jayadratha, Duhshasana, Lakshmana Kumar, and others) to heaven.

attributes.relationship: Duryodhana as leader mourning his fallen army and allies

extraction_text: Duryodhana laments the future grief of his family: his sister Duhshala (upon hearing of her brothers' and husband's deaths), his elderly father Dhritarashtra and mother Gandhari, their daughters-in-law and granddaughters-in-law, and specifically the sorrow of Lakshmana Kumar's mother (his wife).

attributes.relationship: Duryodhana as son, brother, and husband foreseeing family tragedy

extraction_text: Duryodhana expresses a hope that the sage Chyavana, if he learns of these events, will avenge him.

attributes.supernatural_element: Invocation of a sage's potential power

extraction_text: Duryodhana declares that dying at the holy site of Samantapanchaka, he will attain eternal worlds.

attributes.supernatural_element: Belief in attaining heaven due to death at a holy site

extraction_text: After hearing King Duryodhana's lament, thousands of people weep and run in all directions. The earth, seas, forests, and all beings tremble violently with a great sound, and the surroundings grow dark.

attributes.supernatural_element: Cosmic portents (earthquake, darkness) marking the death of a great king

extraction_text: The messengers go to Ashvatthaman and truthfully report the events of the mace duel and the death of King Duryodhana.

attributes.relationship: Messengers inform the Kaurava general of his leader's fate

extraction_text: After reporting everything to Ashvatthaman, the messengers fall silent for a long time, then set out on their return journey, filled with sorrow.
The surviving Kuru warriors (Ashvatthaman, Kripa, and Kritavarman) heard from a messenger that Duryodhana had been killed.
The warriors rushed to the battlefield on fast horses and found Duryodhana lying dead.

attributes.description: Duryodhana's body is described with multiple similes: like a fallen sala tree, a slain elephant, a fallen sun, a dried ocean, a clouded moon, and a fallen tiger

extraction_text: Ashvatthaman, weeping and breathless, laments over Duryodhana's body with a long speech about the transience of life and power.

relationships: Ashvatthaman expresses deep grief for his fallen king and friend

extraction_text: Duryodhana responds with philosophical acceptance of death as ordained by Brahma (the creator).

attributes.philosophical_element: Acceptance of death as part of cosmic order
attributes.divine_reference: Brahma (creator god) established this way of death
relationships: Duryodhana addresses his remaining allies with his dying words

extraction_text: Duryodhana reflects on his life, fate, and death while accepting his fate.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Mention of fate and divine will

extraction_text: Duryodhana expresses that he has won the immortal world according to Vedic standards and acknowledges Krishna's power but states he never abandoned Kshatriya dharma.

attributes.relationships: Duryodhana acknowledges Krishna's power but asserts his own adherence to duty

extraction_text: Duryodhana becomes silent, filled with tears, and is tormented by grief and pain.
Ashvatthama sees Duryodhana weeping and becomes enraged with fury like the fire of universal destruction.

attributes.relationships: Ashvatthama's loyalty and anger toward Duryodhana's suffering

extraction_text: Ashvatthama vows to kill all the Panchalas in front of Krishna by any means necessary, swearing by his religious merits, charity, righteousness, and good deeds.

extraction_text: Duryodhana, pleased by Ashvatthama's words, asks Kripa to bring a water pot for Ashvatthama's consecration as army commander.

extraction_text: After consecration, Ashvatthama embraces Duryodhana and departs with a lion's roar that echoes in all directions.
